claims.text: Combined irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and enhanced defect recombination at nanocrystalline grain boundaries govern structural and chemical stability in refractory high-entropy nanoalloys.
The combined irradiation effects suppress conventional grain coarsening.
The combined irradiation effects suppress precipitation.
The proposed initial material is a nanocrystalline quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf refractory high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The relevant intervention combines temperatures near 1073–1173 K with He and Kr ion irradiation.
The tested dual-beam exposure reaches approximately 8–9 dpa and approximately 9% He.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries act as efficient defect sinks.
Nanocrystalline grain boundaries are sites of ballistic sub-cascade formation that divide larger grains into refined substructures.
Irradiation-induced ballistic mixing dynamically homogenizes the elemental distribution and counteracts segregation and precipitation.
A high density of nanograin boundaries maximizes interstitial-vacancy recombination rates.
The proposed synergy between ballistic mixing and defect recombination maintains or refines grain size during irradiation.
Dual-beam irradiation at high temperature will produce maintained or refined grains relative to the annealed-only baseline.
Dual-beam irradiation will produce minimal elemental segregation and precipitation.
Annealing without irradiation causes modest grain coarsening in the W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf nanoalloy.
Thermally activated diffusion during annealing causes elemental segregation, including possible Hf enrichment at grain boundaries.
The prediction is bounded to irradiation doses up to approximately 9 dpa and approximately 9% He.
The mechanism applies near the order-disorder transition temperatures of refractory high-entropy nanoalloys.
The balance between irradiation-induced mixing and thermal diffusion is sensitive to composition, dose rate, and temperature gradients.
Short-range-order evolution may contribute to stability, but its contribution remains unquantified.
Similar or greater grain coarsening, segregation, or precipitation in the irradiated sample relative to the annealed-only sample would falsify the hypothesis.
